system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2138-03-16 00:00:00 to 2138-03-17 16:00:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted for scheduled flexible bronchoscopy with balloon dilation and bronchial wash due to recurrent tracheal stenosis related to relapsing polychondritis. The procedure was performed without complications, and he remained stable throughout the admission with no respiratory distress or pain. Laboratory results showed leukocytosis, attributed to underlying inflammatory disease rather than infection. He was discharged home with a five-day course of high-dose prednisone, instructions to resume his baseline medications, and follow-up planned with interventional pulmonology in four weeks for review of biopsy and culture results. His breathing improved, and oxygen was successfully weaned prior to discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. ___. I'm Dr. ___, one of your hospital doctors. You're here today for a scheduled bronchoscopy to help with your tracheal stenosis. How are you feeling this morning?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Morning, Doctor. I’m okay, a bit nervous. My breathing’s been a little tight lately, but not worse than usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Your history of relapsing polychondritis has caused narrowing in your airway, and we’re going to do a balloon dilation today to open it up a bit. It’s a routine procedure for you, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve had it a few times before. Last time was in February. It helped for a while, but it’s starting to close up again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ll use a balloon to stretch the narrowed areas in your trachea and possibly the left main bronchus. We’ll also take some biopsies and washings to check for any changes or infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Biopsies? Is something new going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No signs of anything serious, but it’s standard to check. We want to make sure the inflammation isn’t getting worse and rule out infection. You’ve been on tobramycin — that’s to prevent lung infections, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I inhale it twice a day. My pulmonologist said it helps keep the bacteria down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll continue that. Now, your labs this morning show a high white blood cell count — 23.8. But given your condition, that’s likely from inflammation, not infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s been high before. My rheumatologist says it’s from the polychondritis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ll keep an eye on it. You’ll stay overnight for observation after the procedure, just to make sure your breathing stays stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s fine. I’d rather be safe. Any pain expected?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You might have some mild soreness or discomfort in your airway. We’ll give you lidocaine nebulizers and pain meds like Tylenol or tramadol if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. And my oxygen? I’m on 40% through the trach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you on the 40% trach mask today and monitor your saturation. It’s been in the mid-90s, which is acceptable. We’ll do a chest X-ray after the procedure too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. You just came back from the bronchoscopy. Everything went smoothly — they dilated multiple areas in your airway and took biopsies. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Tired. My throat feels raw, and I can taste a little blood. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s expected. The scope and balloon can irritate the airway. We’ll keep you on the trach mask and give you lidocaine nebs to numb it. No fever or chest pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, just the soreness. Breathing feels a bit easier already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good sign. We’ll watch you closely tonight. Your chest X-ray shows the trach tube is in place, and no new issues in the lungs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor, can I drink water yet?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet — we need to wait a few more hours to make sure your throat is healing and you can swallow safely. We’ll reassess in a couple of hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Vital signs are stable, oxygen is 95% on 40% trach. You can try small sips of water now — slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I’ll take it slow. Any news on the washings they took?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Preliminary report shows Serratia marcescens and Proteus mirabilis, but in low amounts. They’re considered part of your normal respiratory flora right now, not an active infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous? I’ve heard of Serratia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be, but in your case, it’s likely just colonizing your airway due to your trach and chronic lung changes. We’ll continue your inhaled tobramycin to keep it in check.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m feeling better. Can I go home tomorrow?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, if you stay stable. We’re keeping you overnight to make sure there’s no bleeding or swelling that could block your airway.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your repeat chest X-ray looks stable — trach tube in place, no pneumonia. Your oxygen is 93% on 40%, and you’re eating and drinking fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. So I can go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re planning to discharge you today. We’re giving you a steroid taper — prednisone — to reduce airway inflammation after the procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Like last time? I remember that helped.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, starting at 40 mg and tapering down over five days. Also, keep taking your regular meds — losartan, famotidine, calcium, and the inhaled tobramycin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Interventional pulmonology will contact you to schedule your next bronchoscopy in about four weeks. They’ll review the biopsy results then.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I start having trouble breathing or cough up more blood?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Come back right away. Also, call your pulmonologist if you have fever, increased mucus, or worsening pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll watch for that. Thanks for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll have your discharge papers ready soon. Rest well at home, and keep that follow-up appointment.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted for observation following a scheduled flexible bronchoscopy with balloon dilation of multi-level airway stenosis due to relapsing polychondritis and Ruvalcaba-Myhre-Smith syndrome. The procedure was completed without complications, and he remained hemodynamically stable throughout the admission, with oxygen saturations in the mid- to high-90s on 40% trach mask. Mild post-procedural pain was managed with analgesics. Bronchial washings showed Serratia marcescens and Proteus mirabilis, interpreted as colonizing flora rather than active infection. Biopsies were obtained and pending at discharge. A prednisone taper was prescribed to reduce inflammation, and he was discharged home with follow-up planned with interventional pulmonology in four weeks.
